items.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: That’s what Cal Collins told me this morning, he said it.

ctx.x: Yeah, sometimes they’re right on and they see things as musicians do or close to it, or they describe things in a very good way, which is a hard thing to do, describing music with words has always been a challenging thing. So I have to give these guys some credit and give them a little leeway. But there’s times when they come up with stuff and it’s like, is he listening to the same thing that I’m listening to? Or they read a lot into things sometimes. But he’s one of the good ones, and I’m honored that he’d say…

Well I like the fact that on your little breaks that you had in there, you didn’t choose to just fill them with a million notes, like sometimes younger players do. That’s what Cal Collins told me this morning, he said it.

Well it’s true. Yeah, I like to play a more, kind of a lean style, and just try and make the notes count a little bit more, you know, the ones that I play. I’ve never been much of the player who tries to play a zillion notes. And I think especially in the older styles or whatever you want to call it — swing or traditional jazz — it’s less appropriate anyway. It just doesn’t sound right when the trumpet player is playing a zillion notes, especially when you’re playing in the ensembles and playing the lead melody.…
